common_name: Mississippi Delta Hosta (Giant Deeply Lobed Cupped-Leaf Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, giving this giant hosta ample room to spread.

directions: Registered in the late 1990s from a cross of 'Sea Gold' and 'Golden Torch', this giant hosta forms a bold mound of broad, deeply veined leaves that cup downward and carry unusually heavy substance for such a large cultivar. Pale lavender flowers rise on tall scapes from early to midsummer, well above the foliage mass. Site it where the mature clump can spread several feet in each direction, since crowding flattens the characteristic cupped leaf form. Keep soil evenly moist and mulch to protect shallow roots through summer heat.

common_name: Tomorrow's Child Bearded Iris (Pastel Pink and Red-Violet Plicata Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Registered by Australian hybridizer Barry Blyth from a cross of 'Lisa Ann' and 'Child of Fortune' and introduced in the early 1980s, this tall bearded iris opens soft pastel pink standards above falls of iridescent red-violet rimmed in a narrow pastel pink border, with a tangerine-red beard and laced, ruffled petal edges. It blooms in midseason to late season on sturdy, well-branched stalks and went on to collect several American Iris Society honors, and was later used itself as a parent of the iris 'In Town'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the old woody center and keeping rhizome tops exposed to the sun.

common_name: Arctic Blast Hosta (Twisted Blue-Green Wavy-Margined Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Bred from a cross of 'Komodo Dragon' and 'Elvis Lives' and registered in 2019, this medium-to-large hosta carries thick, frosted blue-green leaves with pronounced wavy margins and a distinctive twisted tip, their undersides contrastingly white. Pale lavender flowers open in early to midsummer on scapes held above the mound. The heavy leaf substance offers useful resistance to slug damage compared with thinner-leafed hostas. Keep soil consistently moist and mulch to conserve moisture through hot spells.

common_name: Winfield Blue Hosta (Powdery Blue Wavy-Leaf Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light to full shade.

directions: Also distributed under the designation Zilis 99, this hosta arose as a spontaneous tissue-culture mutation and is grown chiefly for its exceptionally good powdery blue leaf color, holding that cast on broadly rounded, wavy-margined foliage better than most comparably sized blue cultivars. Lavender flowers appear on scapes in late summer. It has also produced its own sport, a misted blue-green, white-margined selection distributed separately. Grow in light shade for the best blue coloring, since too much direct sun fades the waxy bloom responsible for the color.

common_name: Red Letter Azalea (Red-Orange Exbury-Strain Deciduous Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; site in dappled shade to morning sun with afternoon shade.

directions: An old Exbury-strain deciduous azalea descended from Lionel de Rothschild's breeding at Exbury Gardens and carried forward through later Knap Hill-related hybridizing programs, Red Letter bears funnel-shaped, two-to-three-inch flowers blending red and orange tones, held in rounded trusses on an upright, vigorous shrub during mid-spring. Like other members of this breeding line it drops its leaves in fall and flowers before or alongside new foliage emerging the following spring, and was itself later used as a parent in the breeding of 'Pink Carousel'. Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic soil with morning sun and afternoon shade, and avoid heavy pruning, since flower buds set on the previous year's growth.

common_name: Le Chapiron Musk Strawberry (First Named Capron Strawberry Strain)

planting.note: Plant runners or divisions in spring in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun.

directions: Documented in French gardens from the 1570s under the name Le Chapiron, this strain is the earliest named cultivar recorded for the musk strawberry and the source of the old common name 'capron' still used for the species. It later entered the royal kitchen gardens of Louis XIV, where it was grown and described by the king's gardener. Fruit is larger than that of the woodland strawberry, with red skin, pale yellow-white flesh, and the strong musky perfume characteristic of the species. Because most musk strawberry stock is single-sexed, plant it alongside a known male clone to ensure reliable fruit set.
sources: historical Potager du Roi, Versailles records
